episodic merely. And this means that in reality he does not
know God, the Almighty and All-present, at all. For to
know this God means, of course, to experience His liberating
and sustaining power and His controlling guidance not only
when we step forth out of the hum of daily life, in infrequent,
alas! too infrequent pauses, which stand out as islands of
repose in the roaring torrent of everyday affairs; but to have
the assurance of His liberating and sustaining power and to
feel the security of His guiding hand in life as a whole, with
its care and responsibility, its sorrow and its guilt. And if
already in our surrender to nature we experience a sense of
liberation through which our cares vanish and anxieties
become silent, it is that nature gives us an intimation of God
who bestows upon us that freedom which enables us in the
midst of the cares of life to live without fretful care and in the
responsibilities of life to feel the burden fall from our
shoulders, since He cares for us and stands forth as the One
who is ultimately responsible for us.
CIV
But such faith is the Christian faith which as such is
awakened by the message of the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
Now this message is a message of forgiveness—a forgiveness
which does not simply mean that God forgives us this or
that moral failing, as among ourselves we can and should
forgive each other our lapses. It declares rather that God
forgives and has forgiven the fundamental sin of our whole
existence, the one essential sin which is that we have
separated ourselves from God and have as it were cut our-
selves off from Him in order to live independently in our own
strength. In Christ He has created a new humanity; the
humanity of those who allow Christ the Good Shepherd to
lead them back to God, the Omnipotent and Omnipresent,
trom whom, to whom, and through whom, are all things.
